title: Epic of Gilgamesh, Tablet VI: Ishtar and the Bull of Heaven
source: British Museum tablet photographs + eBL manuscript transliterations (eBL corpus edition L I.4, Poem of Gilgamesh (ed. A. R. George, rev. G. Rozzi and E. Jiménez), SB VI) + English of the eBL edition (A. R. George (eBL edition))
description: Standard Babylonian Epic of Gilgamesh, Tablet VI: 182 of 183 lines, each shown on a photographed cuneiform tablet (7 tablets), with the eBL transliteration of that tablet and A. R. George's English translation.
introduction:
The goddess Ishtar proposes marriage to Gilgamesh. He rejects her and lists the fates of her former lovers. She asks her father Anu for the Bull of Heaven, which ravages Uruk until Gilgamesh and Enkidu kill it.

The Standard Babylonian version of the epic, traditionally ascribed to the scholar Sin-leqi-unninni, was written on twelve tablets. Most surviving copies come from the libraries of Ashurbanipal at Nineveh (7th century BCE) and from Babylon and other Babylonian cities (7th-2nd century BCE). This page gives Tablet VI in the line numbering of the electronic Babylonian Library edition by A. R. George (2022 and later revisions).

How this page is built. Each section is a run of consecutive lines as written on one photographed clay tablet. For every line the eBL edition (https://www.ebl.lmu.de/corpus/L/1/4/SB/VI) lists the manuscripts that carry it, with each tablet's own column and line numbers; the tablet chosen for each run is the photographed copy of the work with the most signs preserved there. Commentaries and texts that only quote a line are never chosen. School and excerpt tablets are used only for lines that no photographed library copy preserves as well, and only where they carry the line as text; their sections say so. The original text is eBL's transliteration of that tablet's signs (not a modern composite text): square brackets mark broken signs, x an illegible sign, # a damaged sign, ? an uncertain reading, and words in {braces} are determinatives; the notes give a key to every sign used on this page, and eBL's layout codes are written out in words (for example '(line break)' or '(blank space)'). Superscript numbers are the line numbers of the eBL edition, used in both the Akkadian and the English. The English is A. R. George's translation in the eBL edition (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0), one line of English per line of the poem; italics mark uncertain renderings, as in the source. Where the tablet is broken, the English still translates the whole line of eBL's composite text; each section's note names the lines that are broken on its tablet.

Finding a line on the photograph. Each section names the tablet, the face and column, and the tablet's own line numbers (a prime, as in 5', counts from the first preserved line of a broken column). On a tablet with six columns the obverse carries columns i-iii from left to right; the reverse, turned over from bottom to top, carries columns iv-vi from right to left. The photographs often show the obverse above the reverse with the edges around them; a fragment preserves only part of this layout.

This page shows 182 of the 183 lines of the eBL edition (99%), from 7 tablets in the British Museum: K.3990 (Nineveh), K.231 (Nineveh), K.4579.A (Nineveh), Sm.2112 (Nineveh), K.5335 (Nineveh), K.15193 (Nineveh), K.14945 (Nineveh).

Lines not shown. 1 of the 183 lines of the eBL edition are not shown, because no photographed copy of the work used here carries them: 144 (no photograph in eBL: VAT.9667 (Vorderasiatisches Museum, Berlin)). A line is shown only on a photographed tablet that carries it as text. Commentaries and other texts that quote a line (letters, rituals, god lists) are not used as witnesses, because they carry it with explanations or inside another text; tablets without a photograph in eBL are not used, because the line could not be shown on its tablet.
translator_notes: Akkadian: eBL transliteration of the signs on the photographed tablet (manuscript-level ATF), not a composite text.
English: A. R. George's translation in the eBL edition; it renders eBL's composite text, including restorations from other tablets.
Line numbers: eBL edition (based on A. R. George, The Babylonian Gilgamesh Epic, Oxford 2003). Each section also gives the tablet's own column and line numbers.

Signs in the Akkadian: [ ] broken away; x illegible sign; # damaged sign; ? uncertain reading; ! sign corrected by the editor; ... broken signs of unknown number; ( ) signs perhaps broken away; { } determinative; (line break) the line runs on to the next line of the tablet; (blank space) a space left by the scribe.

translation.text:
1He washed his matted hair, he cleaned his equipment,
2he shook his locks down over his back.
3He cast aside his dirty things, he clothed himself with his clean things,
4He wrapped himself in cloaks, tied with a sash.

Photograph checked: obverse, reverse and edges of the join K.3990 + K.4579 + DT.2 + Rm.578 + Rm-II.197 (modern plaster fill, ink numbers on the pieces); text on both faces, consistent with eBL's columns i and iv-vi. The English of these lines translates eBL's composite text, so it includes words that are not preserved on this tablet but are restored from other manuscripts or by the editors. Square brackets in the English mark eBL's restorations in its composite text; words that survive on other tablets carry no brackets even where this tablet is broken. Line 4 is complete on this tablet.

translation.text:
5Gilgameš put on his crown.
6The lady Ištar looked covetously on the beauty of Gilgameš:
7‘Come, Gilgameš, you be the bridegroom!
8Grant me your fruits, I insist!
9You shall be my husband and I will be your wife!
10Let me harness for you a chariot of lapis lazuli and gold,
11whose wheels are gold and whose horns are amber.
12You shall have in harness “storm-lions”, huge mules.
13Come into our house with scents of cedar!
14When you come into our house,
15doorway and throne shall kiss your feet.
16Kings, courtiers and nobles shall be bowed down beneath you,
17Produce of mountain and lowland they shall bring you as tribute!
18Your nanny goats shall bear triplets and your ewes twins,
19your donkey foal under load shall outpace a mule.
20At the chariot your horse shall gallop majestically,
21at the yoke your ox shall acquire no rival.
22[Gilgameš] opened his mouth to speak,
23[saying] to the lady Ištar:
24‘[If indeed I were] to take you in marriage,
25[...] myself and my clothing,
26[whence will come] my food and my sustenance?
27[will you feed me] bread fit for a god?
28[will you pour me ale] fit for a king?
29[...] should I bind,
30[…] should I pile high?
31[Would…] wrap […] in a cloak?
32‘[Why] would I take you in marriage?
33[You, a frost] that congeals no ice,
34a slatted door [that does not] block breeze and draught,

45As for him of… […] his arm.
46To Dumuzi the husband of your youth,
47to him you have allotted perpetual weeping, year on year.
48You loved the speckled allallu-bird,
49you struck him and broke his wing,
50(now) he stands in the woods crying “My wing!”
51You loved the lion, perfect in strength,
52seven and seven pits you have dug for him.
53You loved the horse, famed in battle,
54to him you have allotted whip, spurs and lash.
55To him you have allotted a seven-league gallop,
56to him you have allotted muddy water to drink.
57To his mother Silili you have allotted perpetual weeping.
58You loved the shepherd, the grazier, the herdsman,
59who regularly piled up for you (bread baked in) embers,
60slaughtering kids for you every day.
61You struck him and turned him into a wolf,
62so his own shepherd boys drive him away,
63and his dogs take bites at his thighs.
64You loved Išullānu, your father’s gardener,

79And you would love me and [change me] as (you did) them?’

81Ištar was furious and [went up] to heaven.
82Ištar went [weeping] before her father, Anu,
83her tears flowing before Antu, her mother.

145Then Gilgameš like a butcher [(…)], brave and skilful,
146[pressed home] his knife between the yoke of the horns and the slaughter-spot.
147After they had slain the Bull of Heaven,
148they took its heart and set it before Šamaš.
149They stepped back and prostrated themselves before Šamaš,
150both of them (then) sat down together.
151Ištar went up on to the wall of Uruk-the-Sheepfold,
152she hopped and stamped, she uttered a woeful wail:
153‘Woe to Gilgameš, who vilified me, (who) killed the Bull of Heaven!’
154Enkidu heard this speech of Ištar,
155he tore a haunch off the Bull of Heaven and threw it down before her.
156‘You too, had I caught you, I would have treated you like it!
157I would have draped its guts on your arms!’
158Ištar assembled the courtesans, prostitutes (and harlots),
159she instituted mourning over the Bull of Heaven’s haunch.
160Gilgameš summoned the craftsmen, all the smiths,
161for the craftsmen to praise the thickness of its horns.
162Thirty minas of lapis lazuli each was their mass,
163Two minas each their rims,
164six kor of oil was the capacity of both.
165He dedicated (them) for the anointing of his god, Lugalbanda,
166he took (them) in and hung (them) in his bed-chamber.
167They washed their hands in the River Euphrates,
168they took each other (by the hand) to go forward.
169As they drove along the street of Uruk,
